What Keeps Nuclear Weapons from Proliferating: The hardest step in making a nuclear bomb

That only explains Uranium enrichment, which is (correctly) the problem with getting a Uranium bomb.

He doesn't touch on Plutonium at all there.

Plutonium is a waste product in many Uranium burning power plants, because of that it is much more common (and as there are uranium plants, the plutonium is easier to get to than raw uranium). So aquiring the Plutonium for a bomb is easier.

However, the mechanics of the bomb itself is much much more difficult. Uranium chain reactions produce 2 free neutrons per uranium fission, so the chain reaction doubles. 1 - 2 - 4 - 8 - 16 - 32 - 64 - 128 - 256 - 512 - 1024. So it took 11 generations to get over 1000 fission per generation. Plutonium fission produces 3 free neutrons per fission event. 1 - 3 - 9 - 27 - 81 - 243 - 729 - 2187 so in 8 generations we've reached over 2000 fission events. As you can see the energy is released MUCH faster. That, as it turns out, is a problem. The Plutonium actually burns too fast and will blow itself apart before enough material can undergo fission because of the extra neutron produced per fission event. So in order to make a critical mass that will fully undergo fission before obliterating itself you have to compress the core together PERFECTLY. This is done with "explosive lensing" where ABSOLUTELY PERFECT shaped explosives surrounding the core explode in a manner that uniformly compresses it so it can undergo fission. So actually designing the bomb is insanely hard.

North Korea tried to make a Plutonium bomb, it worked but it also failed as its yield was smaller than expected which makes me think they did not have a properly made core and that caused it to blow apart before most of the core could fissile.

If even a small part of it lags behind the rest, the compression wont be uniform and that "weak spot" will be where the plutonium will "burst out" when it starts to chain react and you'll lose material that wont fissile. Another super interesting thing about Nuclear Weapons has to do with the Nazis and it being "impossible" to make a critical mass.

Before Oppenheimer and his team, the idea of creating a critical mass weapon was known. Doing it with nuclear fission however was considered impossible by pretty much everyone. The problem was, according to the math, in order to get enough Uranium together where the neutrons will collide with a U235 nucleus before they escape the core would require more Uranium than was thought to exist in the whole world. Neutrons are INSANELY tiny and unless they hit the nucleus of an atom they have no affect. The nucleus of the atoms are also INSANELY tiny. So to ensure that the neutron would hit another nucleus you have to have more than a planet's worth of nuclei. This is problematic if you wish to make a bomb.

So during WW2 the Nazis were working on creating a fission bomb as well, and like everyone else they ran into the critical mass problem. The story goes that the department responsible for the project was extremely totalitarian, what the lead Dr. said, went and subordinates were never to question his choices. The physicists I've talked to say this single fact may have been what prevented the Nazi's from beating us to the bomb.

In the US Oppenheimer's team ran into the same problem, however an assistant on the project came up with the idea of using Barium to work as a kind of Mirror around the core that would reflect any escaping neutrons back into the core. This would allow them to reduce the uranium needed from the size of a small city, to the size of a softball. This led to the development of the core used in the bombs themselves.
It really is an amazing accomplishment of physics and engineering.

Chemical explosives are precisely shaped to compress the fissile material. It is insanely hard to get right.
